tactics.claim: Start sending email at all, because the contact is already paid for and the only marginal cost is software and writing time, yielding a reported 35–45x ROI.
tactics.mechanism: Acquisition cost is sunk; email is follow-up on contacts you already own, and delivery is not gated by an algorithm, so incremental revenue comes at near-zero incremental cost.
tactics.evidence: Cited industry ROI range of 35–45x from unnamed sources, plus consumption stats (61% check email multiple times/day, uniform across age brackets). No first-party figures for the ROI claim.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class, but it is essentially exhortation to use a channel Real Skin Care already treats as its primary retention surface — there is no mechanism to execute here beyond 'send email'. The 35–45x figure also presumes a list size and acquisition machine that a $2,700/mo solo operation does not have.

tactics.rejectReason: Pure exhortation to use a channel the business already runs; no executable mechanism, and the ROI multiple assumes list scale that does not exist.

tactics.claim: Make unsubscribing easy and visible rather than hard, because captive-but-dormant subscribers damage long-term domain deliverability more than unsubscribes do.
tactics.mechanism: Continuing to send to an uninterested segment drives down engagement signals and domain reputation, which reduces the odds that the people who do want your email actually receive it in the primary inbox rather than the promotions tab.
tactics.evidence: Practitioner reasoning plus his own numbers: ~1%+ unsubscribe on the first send, now ~0.42% per email. No controlled comparison.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle with a deliverability mechanism that does not depend on scale — in fact a small list is more fragile, since a handful of spam complaints on a sub-1,000-subscriber list can meaningfully hurt inbox placement for the reorder and transition-period emails that attack the 18–22.5% repeat rate. Zero cost, one-time setup for a solo operator. Not higher because the revenue effect is invisible at this volume and Shopify/Klaviyo already include a compliant unsubscribe link by default; the additive work is pruning non-openers and not burying the link.

targetSkill.name: marketing-email-list-health
targetSkill.description: Keeping an owned email list deliverable: visible unsubscribes, pruning dormant subscribers, and interpreting churn metrics.

tactics.claim: Expect an abnormally high unsubscribe rate on the first send after a long dormant stretch — it is pulled-forward churn ('shaking the tree'), not a signal to stop emailing.
tactics.mechanism: Subscribers who would have churned across several months churn all at once when contact resumes, so the spike is a one-time cleanup rather than a recurring cost; refusing to send to avoid it just keeps a dead list dead.
tactics.evidence: His own first send had his highest-ever unsubscribe rate (just over 1%), which settled to ~0.42% per email thereafter. Single-case anecdote.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable retention psychology, age irrelevant, and specifically useful for a solo operator who has almost certainly under-mailed a list where 45–52% of revenue comes from repeat buyers. It removes the main reason the send does not happen and sets the correct expectation so a scary first-send metric does not stop the flow build. Capped at 6 because it is an interpretive rule for a number rather than a mechanism that itself produces revenue.

targetSkill.name: marketing-email-list-health
targetSkill.description: Add the rule that the first send to a dormant list produces a one-time unsubscribe spike that should be expected, not avoided.

tactics.claim: Segment the list on the qualifiers you already collect and send each segment only the content that applies to them, rather than blasting everything to everyone.
tactics.mechanism: Relevance, not copy quality, determines response — an advanced message to a beginner (or vice versa) is dismissed regardless of how well it is written, so matching send to segment raises conversion without changing the email.
tactics.evidence: Cites a HubSpot study claiming a ~760–791% ROI increase from segmentation, plus his own practice of splitting by revenue band. Study not linked or dated.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, and the segment that matters here is obvious and free: first-time buyer vs. repeat buyer vs. never-purchased, plus product interest (deodorant vs. oral care vs. lip balm) across 12 SKUs. That maps directly onto the binding retention constraint. Held to 6 because a list this small fragments fast, the cited multiplier is unverifiable, and Amazon customers (~$1,800/mo) are not on the list at all.

targetSkill.name: marketing-email-list-health
targetSkill.description: Add segmentation on already-collected qualifiers (purchase status, product interest) so each send matches the segment.

tactics.claim: Reward the reader in the first glance — open the email with a self-contained payoff (a quote, a one-line insight) so the act of opening is immediately reinforced, and make sure every send delivers one usable thing so it 'pays for itself'.
tactics.mechanism: Behavior recurs because it was rewarded afterward, not because of what preceded it. If opening reliably produces value, open rate compounds; a single useless send can break the habit and push you into the promotions tab, which is inbox death.
tactics.evidence: Behavioral-reinforcement reasoning applied consistently across two teardowns of his own sends, plus the observation that unopened mail eventually lands in the promo tab. No open-rate data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable retention psychology, age irrelevant, and it fills a real gap: existing skills cover what an email says and how it is built but nothing covers why a subscriber opens the next one. targetSkill.name: marketing-email-engagement-loop

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, free, solo-executable, and it points at a mechanism this business has no coverage for — the click, not just the open. Capped at 6 because it presumes destination content worth clicking to that must be built first, and at ~54 orders/month the lift will not be readable as revenue.

targetSkill.name: marketing-email-engagement-loop

A body-care brand emailing a tiny customer list has no comparable dynamic, and this is a traffic-acquisition play sitting behind the Tracking/CRO/Offer gates.

tactics.rejectReason: No engineerable mechanism and requires audience scale and social distribution the business does not have; also an acquisition play behind the current gates.

tactics.claim: Never reuse a generic copy-pasted CTA across assets — write the CTA and the bridge into it so it is contextually tied to the specific content the reader just consumed.
tactics.mechanism: The whole point of the asset is to raise the likelihood of conversion now or later, and the CTA is the part that does that, so spending the extra minutes to make the ask follow logically from what was just read removes the jarring topic switch that kills the click.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus his own examples (his YouTube CTA for this video is the newsletter; a beginner-topic video would point to Skool; an enterprise-value topic would point to the workshop), and a self-critique of his own email for pitching a workshop after a testimonial lesson. He notes that email 'still did really well', so no clean data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable asset-construction principle, age irrelevant, zero cost, and it lands on email — the live owned surface where the 18–22.5% repeat rate is decided. Concretely: a transition-period education email should bridge to the specific deodorant reorder or refill bundle, not a generic 'shop all.' Held at 6 because the existing skill already enforces one ask and CTA placement; the additive claim is narrower — the bridge sentence and the destination must follow the email's subject matter — and nothing here is measurable at ~54 orders/month.

tactics.claim: Use one repeating value-email skeleton — open with something that rewards the reader for opening, put the contextual CTA in the middle, close with something that rewards them for reading — and send it at least once a month.
tactics.mechanism: Front-loading a payoff makes the open feel worth it, a second payoff at the end trains the reader to finish, and burying the ask in the middle means the CTA rides on attention the content already earned rather than competing with it. A fixed skeleton removes per-send decisions, which is why a low cadence is still sustainable.
tactics.evidence: Presented as the format of his own newsletter, with a walkthrough of one send that 'did really well' and a claim that people screenshotted it. No open, click, or revenue figures; the 'you won't make less money' framing is explicitly hedged.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable asset-structure principle, so age is not the limiter. It fills a real gap: the adopted email skeleton is a promo layout (hero image plus three CTAs) that does not fit an education send, and this is exactly an education-send skeleton with the ask placed mid-body. Free and solo-executable at a once-a-month cadence, on the retention surface carrying 45–52% of revenue. Capped at 5 because Hormozi's 'reward' is a B2B business insight; here it must be usage/education content, and a monthly broadcast is a weaker retention lever than the triggered post-purchase and reorder flows.

tactics.claim: Refresh your organic opt-in and tease a high-value upcoming release to drive newsletter signups.
tactics.mechanism: Anticipation for something genuinely valuable gives the visitor a reason to trade an email address now rather than later.
tactics.evidence: Assertion in the closing plug; he describes 'something very juicy' coming in 30 days without naming it. No opt-in rate data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable in class, but choosing a specific desirable incentive for email capture is already covered in detail by marketing-offer-construction, and the teaser variant assumes a pipeline of newsworthy releases a 12-SKU solo operation does not have.
